title: Faith and works (James 2:14–26)
hookLine: faith without works is dead; Luther found James hard, but all churches read it

cards: It's winter. A neighbor knocks on your door. No coat, and they haven't eaten since yesterday.
You smile warmly and say, I'll be thinking of you. Stay warm. Eat something.
Then you close the door. James paints this scene and asks: what good is that? It's the setup for a paragraph Christians still argue over.
Martin Luther found it hard going. And still, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Bibles all keep it.

teach.h: WARM WORDS AT A CLOSED DOOR.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?"

Then: "Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone." A faith that only talks is like those warm words at the door: it sounds right and changes nothing. James gets sharp: you believe there is one God?
Good. "The devils also believe, and tremble." Knowing the right facts isn't the same as trusting with your life.
Then two examples. Abraham, willing to offer Isaac. And Rahab, the woman in Jericho who hid Israel's spies and sent them out another way.
A patriarch and an outsider. Faith showed itself in what each did.
"For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also."
Why the argument? Paul wrote that a person is justified by faith, apart from works of the law. James writes that a person is justified by works, and not by faith only.

In his 1522 preface to the New Testament, Martin Luther called James a letter of straw, compared with books like Romans. He still kept it in his Bible. Christians read the two side by side differently.

teach.h: FAITH, IF IT HATH NOT WORKS, IS DEAD.
teach.b: Catholic and Orthodox Christians often point to James when they teach that God's grace saves through a faith alive with love and good works.
Protestant churches in Luther's line teach that people are saved by faith alone, and that real faith always gets up and does something, which is how they read James.
James's own point is plain: a faith that never opens the door isn't what he means by faith.

how: Christians read James 2 alongside Paul's letters, and churches often pair Sunday worship with practical service, such as food banks, coat drives and visiting, as faith put to work.

games.q: a neighbor with no coat and no food knocks on your door. you say, stay warm, eat something, and close the door. what does James ask?
games.why: "what doth it profit? Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone."

practice: Think of one need you know about right now, one person: a neighbor, a coworker. Picture the warm words you might say, then one thing your hands could actually do, out of faith or simply out of love: a meal, a ride, a call.
If you pray, ask for the courage to follow through.

wordCard.voice: Works. James's test for living faith: faith without works is dead, the same way a body without breath is dead.

orig.note: Greek: works, deeds, things done. James's word for what faith does.

carryVoice: Your line: faith that works. Warm words, and an open door. See you tomorrow.
